Part 00

The exam pack

You have the formula sheet. What you do not have is the decision procedure that turns a question into an answer. That is this part.

the sheet gives definitions. it never tells you which one to reach for.

read the verb in the question first, the matrix second.

if you are stuck: start with best responses for matrix games. other question types need their own method.

0.1 What the paper is actually asking

In one line

Many questions ask for a solution concept; others ask you to construct a game, design a rule, or interpret a result. Identify the requested output before calculating.

There are only about a dozen procedures in the whole syllabus. The table below is the map. Find the phrase the question uses on the left, run the procedure on the right. Some questions require you to model utilities or design a mechanism, so state your assumptions and verify incentives rather than forcing every question into a memorised template.

Question says…ProcedureWhere
"strategic form of this tree", "how many strategies"Count information sets, multiply action counts, enumerate profiles, trace each to a leaf§1.3
"dominant strategy equilibrium", "is X dominated"Fix the opponent column-by-column, compare rows. Decide strong / weak / very weak by counting how many comparisons are strict§2.1–2.2
"simplify", "which strategies survive"Iterated elimination. Strict first — order does not matter. Weak — say which order you used§2.3
"pure strategy Nash equilibrium", "best response"Underline each player's best replies; a cell with every entry underlined is a PSNE§3.2
"Pareto optimal", "efficient", "which equilibrium is better"Compare payoff vectors component-wise; only strict-in-one, no-worse-in-all counts§3.4
"maxmin", "security value", "guarantee"Row minima → take the max. For player 2 work on their payoff, columns§4.1
"minmax", "force on player i"Column maxima of player i's payoff → take the min§4.2
"value of the game", "saddle point", zero-sumSaddle point if maxmin = minmax. Otherwise mix§4.3
"mixed strategy Nash equilibrium", "randomise"Solve for your probabilities by equalising the opponent's payoffs across their supported actions; then check all unused actions§5.3
"find all equilibria"Support enumeration: PSNE first, then every mixed support pair§5.7
"2 × n" or "m × 2" and no saddle pointGraphical: draw the envelope, read off the active 2 × 2 subgame§5.5
"mediator", "correlated equilibrium", "signal"Write the strategic incentive constraints, one per (recommended, deviation) pair§6.3
"bargaining", "split the surplus", "(F, v)"Maximise (x₁ − v₁)(x₂ − v₂) on the efficient frontier§7.2
"characteristic function", "coalition", "v(C)"Cooperative. Which concept? core, imputation, or Shapley — read on§8–10
"core", "can coalition C block"Σ over N equals v(N); Σ over every C is at least v(C)§9.1
"Shapley value", "fair share", "power index"Marginal contributions weighted by |C|!(n−|C|−1)!/n!§10.1
Where the marks go

The papers ask for clear stepwise reasoning and interpretation. Show your method so your reasoning can be assessed; the exact partial-credit allocation is not provided. Write the comparison you are making before you make it: "u₁(C, NC) = −1 > u₁(NC, NC) = −2" is worth more than "C dominates".

0.2 Decoding the notation on the sheet

The formula sheet is dense because it is compressed, not because it is hard. Six symbols carry almost all of it.

SymbolRead it asTrap
Γ = ⟨N, (Sᵢ), (uᵢ)⟩"players, what each can do, what each gets"(Sᵢ) is shorthand for the whole list S₁,…,Sₙ, not one set
s = (s₁,…,sₙ)one cell of the matrix — a strategy profilea profile is a full specification, one strategy per player
−i"everybody except i"s₋ᵢ is a profile, so for n = 2 it is a single strategy; for n = 3 it is a pair
(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ)the same cell, written so you can vary i's partit is not a new object — it is s with the spotlight on i
bᵢ : S₋ᵢ → 2^Sᵢbest response correspondence — returns a set2^Sᵢ is the power set. Ties mean more than one best reply
σᵢ ∈ Δ(Sᵢ)a probability distribution over i's pure strategiesΔ(Sᵢ) is the simplex; a pure strategy is a corner of it
The one that costs marks

The sheet writes the Nash condition as uᵢ(s*ᵢ, s₋ᵢ) ≥ uᵢ(sᵢ, s*₋ᵢ). That printing has a typo you should mentally correct: the left side must be uᵢ(s*ᵢ, s*₋ᵢ). Both sides hold the others at equilibrium; only i's own strategy varies. If you ever let s₋ᵢ vary too you are testing a dominant strategy, not a Nash equilibrium.

0.3 The eight mistakes that cost marks

#MistakeFix
1Reading player 2's payoff off the wrong number in (a, b)Always (row player, column player). Write "u₂" beside the second number once, at the top of the answer
2Calling a weak dominance "strong"Strong needs > in every column. One tie kills it
3Equalising your own payoffs when solving for your own mixtureYour probabilities are set by making the opponent indifferent
4Forgetting the pure equilibria when asked for "all" equilibriaPSNE are MSNE with degenerate support. List them first
5Using maxmin rows for player 2Player 2's maxmin scans columns of u₂. Transpose mentally or literally
6Mixing up minmax and maxminmaxmin = what I can guarantee myself. minmax = what they can hold me to. Always v̲ᵢ ≤ v̄ᵢ
7Checking core membership only against singletonsEvery non-empty C ⊆ N, including the two-player coalitions, which is where cores usually fail
8Dropping the empty coalition term in ShapleyC = ∅ contributes v({i}) − v(∅) with weight (n−1)!/n! = 1/n
check — before you go further

A cell is (3, 5). Player 2 deviates and lands on (1, 6). Was the original a Nash equilibrium?

No. Player 2 improved from 5 to 6 by a unilateral deviation, so the profile fails 2's best-response condition. Player 1's fall from 3 to 1 is irrelevant — Nash only insures against unilateral moves.

If s* is a strongly dominant strategy equilibrium, is it a Nash equilibrium?

Yes, always. Dominance is best response against every s₋ᵢ; Nash only demands it against s*₋ᵢ. The converse fails.

Part 01

Reading a game

Before any solution concept: what object is on the page, and what is the complete list of things each player could do?

a strategy is a plan, not a move. that distinction is the whole of §1.3.

|S₂| = 2 × 2 = 4 for a tree with two info sets and two actions each. count sets, not nodes.

dotted line between nodes = one information set = the player cannot tell them apart.

1.1 Strategic form: the tuple

In one line

A strategic form game is three lists — who plays, what each can do, what each gets — and the payoff matrix is just those three lists drawn as a grid.

Formally, Γ = ⟨N, (Sᵢ)ᵢ∈N, (uᵢ)ᵢ∈N⟩ with N = {1,…,n}, strategy sets Sᵢ, and utilities uᵢ : S₁ × ⋯ × Sₙ → ℝ. "Strategic form", "normal form" and "matrix game" all mean the same thing. Everyone chooses simultaneously; nobody sees anyone else's choice first.

For two players the whole game fits in a bimatrix, rows for player 1 and columns for player 2, each cell holding the pair (u₁, u₂). Extracting the tuple from a matrix is a common opening part-question and is worth doing carefully because it is free marks:

1 \ 2AB
A10, 100, 0
B0, 01, 1
the tuple, read off the grid N = {1, 2}; S₁ = S₂ = {A, B} u₁(A,A) = 10; u₁(A,B) = 0; u₁(B,A) = 0; u₁(B,B) = 1 u₂(A,A) = 10; u₂(A,B) = 0; u₂(B,A) = 0; u₂(B,B) = 1

This particular game is a common payoff game — both players get the same number in every cell — and a coordination game, because the good outcomes require agreement. Recognising a named game buys you the answer before you compute it, which is why §1.5 is worth memorising.

Symmetry

A two-player game is symmetric when S₁ = S₂ and u₁(s₁, s₂) = u₂(s₂, s₁) for all pairs. Practically: transpose the matrix and swap the two numbers in each cell; if you get the original back, it is symmetric. Symmetry is worth spotting because it halves your work — whatever you prove for player 1 holds for player 2 by relabelling.

1.2 Extensive form: trees, histories, information sets

The extensive form keeps what the matrix throws away: who moves when, and what they know when they move. The sheet's Definition 1 lists six components. Here is what each one is, on a tree you can picture.

ComponentWhat it isMatching pennies, player 1 first
Nthe players{1, 2}
Aᵢevery action label i ever usesA₁ = A₂ = {H, T}
Hterminal histories — full root-to-leaf paths{HH, HT, TH, TT}
SHproper subhistories, including the empty one ε{ε, H, T}
P : SH → Nwhose turn it is after each subhistoryP(ε)=1, P(H)=2, P(T)=2
Iᵢinformation sets — decision nodes i cannot tell apartI₁={{ε}}, I₂={{H},{T}}
uᵢ : H → ℝpayoff at each leafu₁(HH)=1, u₁(HT)=−1, …
The whole point of an information set

Nodes joined by a dotted line form one information set: the player who moves there knows they are at one of those nodes but not which. Two consequences follow and both are examinable. First, every node in an information set must offer the same action set — otherwise the player could tell them apart by looking at the menu. Second, a strategy must prescribe one action per information set, not per node.

If every information set is a singleton the game has perfect information — everybody always knows exactly where they are. If even one information set has two or more nodes, the game has imperfect information. Matching pennies with observation (MPO) is perfect; matching pennies without observation (MPWO) is imperfect, and its single two-node information set for player 2 is exactly what makes it a simultaneous game in disguise.

Lab 1 · Game tree → strategic form

1.3 Converting a tree to a matrix

In one line

A strategy is a complete contingent plan — one action at every information set you own, including ones you will never reach — so the number of strategies is the product of the action counts, not the sum.

The sheet's Definition 2 says a strategy is a map sᵢ : Iᵢ → Aᵢ with sᵢ(J) ∈ C(J). Unpacked, that is the six-step procedure below. It is the single most mechanical thing in the course and it appears on every paper.

EFG → SFG, six steps 1. List the players. 2. For each player, list their information sets (not nodes). 3. |Sᵢ| = m₁ × m₂ × ⋯ × m_k where m_j = |C(J_j)|, the actions at set J_j. 4. Name each strategy by the action at each set, in a fixed order: "xy". 5. For every profile, trace root → leaf and copy the payoff pair. 6. Draw the grid: rows = S₁, columns = S₂.

Worked: matching pennies with observation

Player 1 has one information set {ε} with actions {H, T}, so |S₁| = 2. Player 2 has two information sets, {H} and {T}, each with two actions, so |S₂| = 2 × 2 = 4. Write player 2's strategy as xy where x is the reply to H and y the reply to T.

1 \ 2HHHTTHTT
H1, −11, −1−1, 1−1, 1
T−1, 11, −1−1, 11, −1

Trace one cell to see the mechanism. Profile (T, HT): player 1 plays T, so we go down the T branch; player 2's strategy says "reply H after H, reply T after T", and we are after T, so player 2 plays T. Terminal history TT, payoff (1, −1). The H half of player 2's plan was never used — but it still had to be specified, and that is exactly why |S₂| is 4 and not 2.

Failure mode

Counting nodes instead of information sets. In MPWO player 2 has two decision nodes but they sit in one information set, so |S₂| = 2, not 4, and the matrix collapses to the familiar 2 × 2 simultaneous game. Getting this wrong changes the size of your answer grid, which is very visible to a marker.

The direction that does not reverse

Every extensive form game has exactly one strategic form (up to renaming strategies). The reverse is false: a single matrix corresponds to many trees, because the matrix has forgotten the timing. That asymmetry is a standard one-mark bookwork question — "every EFG has a unique SFG; a given SFG may come from several EFGs".

check

A player has three information sets, with 2, 3 and 2 available actions. How many pure strategies?

2 × 3 × 2 = 12.

In the entry game, why does the incumbent have only two strategies rather than four?

The incumbent has a single information set — the one reached after "in". "Out" ends the game without giving them a move, so there is nothing else to plan for. S₂ = {accept, fight}.

Two profiles (DG, E) and (DH, F) both lead to terminal history (D). Is that a contradiction?

No. Once player 1 plays D the game ends, so everything downstream is unreached. Several distinct profiles can map to one outcome; the map O(s) from profiles to outcomes is not injective.

About eight games account for most exam questions. Each has a signature payoff pattern and a known answer. Learn to recognise the pattern; you will often be able to write the equilibrium down and spend your time on the justification instead.

GameMatrixSignatureSolution
Prisoner's dilemma(−2,−2) (−10,−1) / (−1,−10) (−5,−5)Defect strictly dominates; both worse off than mutual cooperationStrongly dominant SE at (C, C); Pareto-dominated by (NC, NC)
Battle of the sexes(2,1) (0,0) / (0,0) (1,2)Coordinate, but disagree on whereTwo PSNE (A,A), (B,B); MSNE σ₁=(⅔,⅓), σ₂=(⅓,⅔)

The three continuous ones

These three appear as short-answer questions rather than matrices, because the strategy sets are infinite.

Tragedy of the commons — n farmers, each keeps a sheep (1) or not (0) uᵢ(s₁,…,sₙ) = sᵢ − (5/n) Σⱼ sⱼ = ((n−5)/n)·sᵢ − (5/n) Σj≠i sⱼ n < 5 → (0,…,0) strongly dominant n = 5 → every profile very weakly dominant n > 5 → (1,…,1) strongly dominant, and everyone is worse off for it With a pollution tax of 5 per sheep: (0,…,0) dominant for every n.
Duopoly pricing — firms set p₁, p₂, unit cost c, undercutting takes the market uᵢ(p₁,p₂) = (pᵢ − c)·xᵢ(p₁,p₂), demand split when prices tie PSNE: (c, c) — both price at cost, both earn zero. Why: any pᵢ > c is undercut; any pᵢ < c loses money on every unit.
Sealed-bid auctions — valuations vᵢ, bids bᵢ, ties broken by lowest index uᵢ(b) = yᵢ(b)·(vᵢ − tᵢ(b)) First price: winner pays own bid → shade below vᵢ; truth is NOT dominant. Second price: winner pays second-highest bid → bᵢ = vᵢ is weakly dominant. Worked: v = (20, 20, 16, 16), b = (10, 12, 8, 14). Winner is bidder 4. FPA: t₄ = 14, u₄ = 16 − 14 = 2. SPA: t₄ = 12, u₄ = 16 − 12 = 4.
Braess's paradox, in one paragraph

1000 vehicles route S→T through hub A or hub B. Fixed legs cost 25 min; congested legs cost m/50 min with m vehicles. Split 500/500 and everyone takes 35 min. Add a zero-cost link A→B and the new strategy AB strictly dominates both A and B, so all 1000 take it — and every vehicle now takes 40 min. Adding capacity made everyone worse off, because the dominant-strategy equilibrium is not the efficient profile.

check

Second-price auction, valuations v = (30, 25, 40), bids b = (30, 25, 40). Who wins, what do they pay, what is their utility?

Bidder 3 wins with 40, pays the second-highest bid 30, utility 40 − 30 = 10. Bidders 1 and 2 get 0.

Tragedy of the commons with n = 7. What is the equilibrium and is it efficient?

n > 5, so (1,…,1) is a strongly dominant strategy equilibrium: everyone keeps a sheep. Each gets 1 − 5(7)/7 = −4. Nobody keeping a sheep would give everyone 0, so the equilibrium is Pareto-dominated — the tragedy.

Part 02

Dominance

The strongest thing you can say about a strategy, and the three grades of it that the sheet distinguishes by exactly one inequality sign.

strong = > everywhere. weak = ≥ everywhere and > somewhere. very weak = ≥ everywhere, nothing more.

dominated ≠ dominant. one is a strategy you throw away, the other is one you always play.

strict elimination is order-independent. weak elimination is not — say which order you used.

2.1 The three grades, told apart

In one line

Fix the opponents, compare two of your own rows across every column: all strict is strong, all weak with at least one strict is weak, all weak with no strict required is very weak.

The sheet gives Definitions 5, 8 and 11 as three near-identical displays. Read side by side they differ only in the quantifier attached to the strict inequality:

GradeCondition on s′ᵢ vs sᵢStrictnessUniqueness
Strongly dominatesuᵢ(s′ᵢ, s₋ᵢ) > uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ) ∀ s₋ᵢstrict in every columna strictly dominant strategy is unique if it exists
Weakly dominates≥ ∀ s₋ᵢ, and > for some s₋ᵢat least one strictneed not be unique
Very weakly dominates≥ ∀ s₋ᵢnone requiredoften several; ties count

The nesting is worth stating explicitly because a question often asks for the strongest applicable grade: strong ⟹ weak ⟹ very weak. If two rows are identical, each very weakly dominates the other and neither weakly dominates the other.

The comparison, done properly

Prisoner's dilemma, standard payoffs. To show C strongly dominates NC for player 1, take player 2's strategies one at a time and compare player 1's two rows:

column by column, player 1 2 plays NC: u₁(C, NC) = −1 > u₁(NC, NC) = −2 ✓ strict 2 plays C: u₁(C, C) = −5 > u₁(NC, C) = −10 ✓ strict Both strict → C strongly dominates NC. By symmetry the same holds for player 2. ⇒ (C, C) is a strongly dominant strategy equilibrium.

Now change one payoff so that one comparison ties. With u₁(NC, C) = −10 → −2 and the matrix (−2,−2) (−10,−2) / (−2,−10) (−5,−5):

the same comparison, one tie 2 plays NC: u₁(C, NC) = −2 ≥ u₁(NC, NC) = −2 — equal, not strict 2 plays C: u₁(C, C) = −5 > u₁(NC, C) = −10 ✓ strict Weak everywhere, strict somewhere → C weakly dominates NC. Not strongly.
Failure mode

Declaring strong dominance after checking only the column where the gap is obvious. The definition is universally quantified: one tie in any column, anywhere, demotes it to weak. Write out every column comparison — for a 2 × n game that is n lines and it is where the method marks live.

2.2 Dominant strategies and dominant strategy equilibria

A strategy s*ᵢ is dominant (of a given grade) if it dominates every other strategy of player i, at that grade. A profile (s*₁,…,s*ₙ) is a dominant strategy equilibrium if every player's component is dominant.

Why this matters more than Nash

A dominant strategy is a best response against every profile of the others — you do not have to predict anybody. Nash only demands a best response against the specific equilibrium profile. So a DSE is a far stronger prediction, which is exactly why it so rarely exists.

Both PD variants above give DSE. The very weak case is stranger and worth seeing once, because it produces an equilibrium at every cell. Take (−2,−2) (−5,−2) / (−2,−10) (−5,−10): player 1's two rows tie in both columns, and so do player 2's two columns. Every strategy very weakly dominates every other, so all four profiles are very weakly dominant strategy equilibria.

Second-price auction: the canonical weak DSE

Bidding your true valuation, bᵢ = vᵢ, is weakly dominant in a second-price sealed-bid auction. The proof splits on whether you would win:

bidder 1, let M = max(b₂,…,bₙ) Case v₁ ≥ M: bid v₁ → win, pay M, u₁ = v₁ − M ≥ 0. Bidding higher: still win, still pay M. Same. Bidding below M: lose, u₁ = 0 ≤ v₁ − M. Worse or equal. Case v₁ < M: bid v₁ → lose, u₁ = 0. Bidding above M: win, pay M, u₁ = v₁ − M < 0. Strictly worse. Never worse, sometimes strictly better ⇒ weakly dominant. Not strongly: when you lose either way the payoff ties at 0.

2.3 Iterated elimination

In one line

Delete a dominated strategy, then look again — a strategy that survived the first pass may be dominated in the smaller game, and repeating until nothing moves often leaves a single cell.

Write S¹ᵢ = Sᵢ, and at each round remove every strictly dominated strategy to get S^{k+1}ᵢ ⊆ S^kᵢ. Finite games terminate. The surviving profiles are said to survive iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS).

Worked: a 3 × 3 needing a mixed dominator

1 \ 2XYZ
A3, 10, 10, 0
B0, 14, 10, 0
C1, 11, 15, 0
round by round Round 1 — player 2: u₂(·, X) = u₂(·, Y) = 1 > u₂(·, Z) = 0 in every row. Z strictly dominated by X (and by Y). Delete Z. Round 2 — player 1, now on {X, Y} only: C is not dominated by A (1 > 0 at X fails: A gives 3, C gives 1 at X; at Y, A gives 0, C gives 1 — neither dominates) nor by B. But the mixture ½A + ½B gives at X: ½(3) + ½(0) = 1.5 > 1 ✓ at Y: ½(0) + ½(4) = 2.0 > 1 ✓ C is strictly dominated by a mixed strategy. Delete C. Round 3 — nothing further. Survivors: {A, B} × {X, Y}.
Two facts that get asked directly

Strict elimination is order-independent — whatever order you delete in, the surviving set is the same. Weak elimination is not: different orders can leave different games, and can delete Nash equilibria. So if a question lets you eliminate weakly dominated strategies, state the order you used and note that the outcome depends on it.

Note also that C was not dominated by any mixture in the original game — deleting Z is what made the mixed dominance appear. Elimination can create dominance that was not there before; it never destroys strict dominance.

Lab 2 · Iterated elimination stepper
check

A pure strategy is not dominated by any other pure strategy. Can it still be deleted?

Yes — it may be strictly dominated by a mixture of the others, as C was above. Always test mixtures before concluding a strategy survives.

Does IESDS ever delete a Nash equilibrium?

No. A strictly dominated strategy is never a best response, so it cannot appear in any Nash equilibrium, pure or mixed. Iterated weak elimination can and does delete equilibria.

After IESDS a unique profile remains. Is it a Nash equilibrium?

Yes. Any game has at least one equilibrium (in mixed strategies), none can have been deleted, and only one profile is left — so it is the equilibrium, and it is pure.

Part 03

Pure strategy Nash equilibrium

The workhorse. Twenty seconds of underlining answers most of what the paper asks.

best response is a set. ties are normal, and they are where extra equilibria hide.

underline player 1's best reply in each column, player 2's in each row. both underlined = PSNE.

"no PSNE" is a legitimate answer. matching pennies has none. say so and move to mixing.

3.1 Best response correspondence

In one line

bᵢ(s₋ᵢ) is the set of strategies that maximise i's payoff given what everyone else does, and a profile is a Nash equilibrium exactly when every player's component lies in their own best-response set.

Sheet, Definition 15 bᵢ(s₋ᵢ) = { sᵢ ∈ Sᵢ : uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ) ≥ uᵢ(s′ᵢ, s₋ᵢ) ∀ s′ᵢ ∈ Sᵢ } (s*₁, …, s*ₙ) is a PSNE ⟺ s*ᵢ ∈ bᵢ(s*₋ᵢ) for every i.

The codomain is 2^Sᵢ, the power set — it is a correspondence, not a function, because ties give several best replies at once. That is not a technicality: in the tragedy of the commons with n = 5 every player's best-response set is {0, 1} for every profile of the others, so every profile is a Nash equilibrium.

Battle of the sexes, written out

u: (2,1) (0,0) / (0,0) (1,2) b₁(A) = {A} since u₁(A,A) = 2 > u₁(B,A) = 0 b₁(B) = {B} since u₁(B,B) = 1 > u₁(A,B) = 0 b₂(A) = {A} since u₂(A,A) = 1 > u₂(A,B) = 0 b₂(B) = {B} since u₂(B,B) = 2 > u₂(B,A) = 0 A ∈ b₁(A) and A ∈ b₂(A) → (A, A) is a PSNE B ∈ b₁(B) and B ∈ b₂(B) → (B, B) is a PSNE (A, B): A ∉ b₁(B) and B ∉ b₂(A) → not an equilibrium

3.2 The underline method, and a workbench

In practice nobody writes out best-response sets under exam time. The equivalent, and the thing to do on the paper first:

the twenty-second procedure 1. Go down each column. Underline the largest first number. (player 1's best reply) 2. Go across each row. Underline the largest second number. (player 2's best reply) 3. Any cell with both numbers underlined is a pure strategy Nash equilibrium. 4. Ties: underline all of them. Every fully-underlined cell counts.

The workbench below runs that procedure and everything downstream of it. Type any bimatrix up to 4 × 4 into it, or load a preset. It reports best responses, all three grades of dominance, the pure equilibria, both security values for both players, saddle points, and the mixed equilibrium when the reduced game is 2 × 2. It computes each of those from the numbers in the grid — nothing is hard-coded — so you can use it to check your own working on a past paper.

Lab 3 · Bimatrix workbench
player 1 best reply player 2 best reply pure Nash equilibrium
Reading the workbench

Zero-sum mode locks player 2's payoff to −u₁, so you only fill one number per cell. That is the convention the "Rose and Colin" material on the slides uses, and it is how any question phrased in terms of a value will be set.

3.3 How PSNE relates to dominance

ClaimTrue?Why
Every dominant strategy equilibrium is a PSNEyesBest response against everything includes best response against the equilibrium profile
Every PSNE is a dominant strategy equilibriumnoBoS has two PSNE and no dominant strategies at all
A strictly dominated strategy can appear in a PSNEnoIt is never a best response to anything
A weakly dominated strategy can appear in a PSNEyesIt can tie as a best response against the specific equilibrium profile
Every finite game has a PSNEnoMatching pennies has none. Every finite game does have a mixed one

3.4 Pareto comparisons between equilibria

In one line

Outcome B Pareto-dominates A when nobody is worse off in B and at least one player is strictly better off; an outcome nothing dominates is Pareto-optimal.

The test is component-wise on payoff vectors and takes seconds. What it is not is "higher total" — a bigger sum with one player worse off is not a Pareto improvement.

GamePSNE payoffsVerdict
Battle of the sexes(3,1) and (1,3)Incomparable — each player prefers a different one. Both Pareto-optimal.
Pure coordination(5,5) and (2,2)(5,5) dominates. (2,2) is inefficient — Pareto-ranked.
Anti-coordination(2,1) and (1,2)Incomparable. Both optimal.
Safe / risky(6,6) and (4,2)(6,6) dominates on both coordinates. (4,2) discarded.
Three-equilibrium game(8,1), (5,5), (2,10)All three mutually incomparable — all Pareto-optimal.
Prisoner's dilemma(−5,−5) onlyThe unique equilibrium is Pareto-dominated by the non-equilibrium (−2,−2).
Failure mode

Comparing (8,1) and (5,5) and calling the second "better because 10 > 9". Sum is not the criterion. Player 1 strictly prefers (8,1), so no Pareto ranking exists between them. The prisoner's dilemma is the standard demonstration that equilibrium and efficiency are different questions.

check

Two PSNE give (4, 4) and (4, 6). Which is Pareto-optimal?

Only (4, 6). Player 1 is indifferent and player 2 is strictly better, which satisfies the definition — no-worse-for-all, strictly-better-for-one.

Is a Pareto-optimal outcome necessarily an equilibrium?

No. (NC, NC) in the prisoner's dilemma is Pareto-optimal and is not an equilibrium. The two properties are logically independent.

Find all PSNE of (4,1) (0,4) / (1,5) (1,1).

None. Column A: player 1 prefers A (4 > 1). Row A: player 2 prefers B (4 > 1). Column B: player 1 prefers B (1 > 0). Row B: player 2 prefers A (5 > 1). The best replies cycle, so no cell has both underlined.

Part 04

Security: maxmin, minmax, saddle points

What you can guarantee yourself, what they can hold you to, and when those two numbers coincide.

maxmin: row minima, then the biggest. minmax: column maxima, then the smallest.

for player 2 you do the same thing to u₂ — but scanning columns, not rows. transpose first if it helps.

v̲ᵢ ≤ v̄ᵢ ≤ (payoff at any PSNE). memorise the chain; it answers several one-markers.

4.1 Maxmin — the security value

In one line

Assume the worst about everyone else, and pick the strategy whose worst case is best. The number you end up with is guaranteed to you no matter what anyone does.

Sheet, Definition 16 v̲ᵢ = max(sᵢ ∈ Sᵢ) min(s₋ᵢ ∈ S₋ᵢ) uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ) Procedure (player 1, reading u₁): for each ROW, write the smallest entry → the row minima circle the LARGEST of those → v̲₁, and the row is a maxmin strategy

The maxmin value is the security value: it protects your worst-case payoff. It does not eliminate hindsight regret; after seeing the opponent’s action, another action might have earned more. A Nash strategy carries no such guarantee — if the others deviate from equilibrium, your payoff can fall below your equilibrium payoff.

Worked: the intrusion-detection game

Administrator chooses High or Low security; attacker chooses Attack or Not. Entries are the administrator's uptime in hours, with the attacker's payoff second.

Admin \ AttackerAttackNot attackrow min
High security8, −510, 08
Low security2, −212, 02
both players Admin: min(8, 10) = 8 ; min(2, 12) = 2 ; max(8, 2) = 8 v̲₁ = 8, maxmin strategy = High security. Guarantee: at least 8 hours uptime whatever the attacker does. Attacker: work on u₂ down the COLUMNS of the attacker's own payoffs. Attack: min(−5, −2) = −5 Not attack: min( 0, 0) = 0 max(−5, 0) = 0 ⇒ v̲₂ = 0, maxmin strategy = Not attack.
Failure mode

Computing player 2's maxmin by taking row minima of u₂. Player 2 chooses columns, so the min is taken over player 1's choices, i.e. down each column of the u₂ matrix. Getting this backwards is the single most common maxmin error and it usually produces a plausible-looking wrong number.

4.2 Minmax — what can be forced on you

Sheet, Definition 17 v̄ᵢ = min(s₋ᵢ ∈ S₋ᵢ) max(sᵢ ∈ Sᵢ) uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ) Procedure (player 1's minmax, reading u₁): for each COLUMN, write the largest entry → the column maxima circle the SMALLEST of those → v̄₁ the column achieving it is the others' minmax strategy against player 1

Note the asymmetry in who the strategy belongs to. The maxmin strategy is yours; the minmax strategy profile is theirs, chosen to punish you. Questions phrase this as "what is the minmax strategy of player 2 against player 1" — the answer is a strategy of player 2.

Worked: the non-symmetric company game

1 \ 2ABrow min (u₁)
A4, 10, 40
B1, 51, 11
col max (u₁)41
player 1 maxmin: row minima 0 and 1 → v̲₁ = 1, maxmin strategy B. minmax: column maxima 4 and 1 → v̄₁ = 1, forced by player 2 playing B. Here v̲₁ = v̄₁ = 1. player 2 (read u₂ = 1, 4 / 5, 1) maxmin: column minima A: min(1,5) = 1 ; B: min(4,1) = 1 → v̲₂ = 1. minmax: row maxima A: max(1,4) = 4 ; B: max(5,1) = 5 → v̄₂ = 4, forced by player 1 playing A. This game has no PSNE — check by underlining and watch the best replies cycle.
The chain to memorise

For every player i, in any strategic form game: v̲ᵢ ≤ v̄ᵢ. And if a pure Nash equilibrium s* exists, uᵢ(s*) ≥ v̄ᵢ ≥ v̲ᵢ. Equilibrium pays you at least what can be forced on you, which is at least what you can guarantee yourself. Several one-mark true/false questions are answered directly by this chain.

Lab 4 · Security values and saddle points

4.3 Saddle points and the value of a zero-sum game

In one line

An entry that is simultaneously the smallest in its row and the largest in its column is a saddle point, and when one exists both players should play through it and the game has a value in pure strategies.

The convention here is the "Rose and Colin" one from the slides: a single matrix, entries are payoffs to Rose (the row player), and Colin's payoff is the negative. Rose maximises, Colin minimises.

Rose \ ColinABCDrow min
A42522
B21−1−20−20
C32422
D−160161−16
col max42162
reading it off maxmin over rows = max(2, −20, 2, −16) = 2 minmax over cols = min(4, 2, 16, 2) = 2 They agree ⇒ value v = 2, and the four cells (A,B), (A,D), (C,B), (C,D) are saddle points. (B, A) is not — 2 is not the largest in column A.

When maxmin and minmax disagree there is no saddle point, no pure solution, and the players must randomise. That is Part 05.

Where the numbers come from

Saddle points survive any order-preserving relabelling of the payoffs, so ordinal utilities are enough to find one. Mixed strategies are different: the mixture weights are ratios of payoff differences, so they require cardinal utilities — an interval scale, unique up to a positive linear transformation au + b with a > 0. That is the whole content of the utility-theory module, and it is why the lottery-elicitation procedure exists.

check

A zero-sum game has maxmin 3 and minmax 7. What can you conclude?

No saddle point, so no pure solution. The value lies somewhere in [3, 7] and is attained by mixed strategies.

Rescale every payoff by u ↦ 3u + 10. What changes?

Saddle points, dominance relations and equilibrium locations are unchanged — this is a positive linear transformation, so it preserves cardinal utilities. The value changes to 3v + 10, and mixing probabilities are unchanged because they depend only on ratios of differences.

Why can a game have several saddle points but only one value?

All saddle points carry the same payoff. If two saddle entries differed, one would violate the row-minimum or column-maximum condition against the other's row/column.

Sheet: Definitions 16–17, Theorem 1. Slides: Maxmin/Minmax; Utility Theory.

Part 05

Mixed strategy Nash equilibrium

Where most of the marks are. Four methods, and knowing which one the question wants.

you solve for your probabilities by equalising their payoffs. this is the one everybody gets backwards.

support = the strategies you actually play with positive probability.

2×2 → best responses and indifference. zero-sum 2×n or m×2 → graph. equalise all only as a candidate, then verify the support.

zero-sum 2×2 has a shortcut: oddments. use it, then verify.

5.1 Mixed strategies, supports, expected payoffs

Sheet, Definitions 18, 21, 22 σᵢ : Sᵢ → [0,1] with Σ(sᵢ ∈ Sᵢ) σᵢ(sᵢ) = 1 — a mixed strategy δ(σᵢ) = { sᵢ ∈ Sᵢ : σᵢ(sᵢ) > 0 } — its support δ(σ) = δ(σ₁) × ⋯ × δ(σₙ) — support of a profile uᵢ(σᵢ, σ₋ᵢ) = Σ(sᵢ) σᵢ(sᵢ) · uᵢ(sᵢ, σ₋ᵢ) uᵢ(sᵢ, σ₋ᵢ) = Σ(s₋ᵢ) ( Π(j≠i) σⱼ(sⱼ) ) · uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ)

A pure strategy is a degenerate mixed strategy e(sᵢ) putting probability 1 on one action. Δ(Sᵢ), the set of all mixtures, is called the mixed extension. Randomisations across players are assumed independent, which is exactly the assumption that correlated equilibrium (Part 06) drops.

Support questions are free marks. Given σ₁(a)=0.2, σ₁(b)=0.5, σ₁(c)=0.3, σ₁(d)=0 and σ₂(a)=0.6, σ₂(b)=0, σ₂(e)=0.4, σ₂(f)=0: the supports are δ(σ₁)={a,b,c} and δ(σ₂)={a,e}, and δ(σ) is their Cartesian product — six profiles.

5.2 The indifference theorem

In one line

If you are willingly mixing, every pure strategy in your support must give you exactly the same expected payoff — otherwise you would shift all your probability onto the better one.

Sheet, Theorem 2 — necessary and sufficient for MSNE (σ*₁,…,σ*ₙ) is a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium ⟺ for every player i: (1) uᵢ(sᵢ, σ*₋ᵢ) is the SAME for all sᵢ ∈ δ(σ*ᵢ) (2) uᵢ(sᵢ, σ*₋ᵢ) ≥ uᵢ(s′ᵢ, σ*₋ᵢ) for all sᵢ ∈ δ(σ*ᵢ), all s′ᵢ ∉ δ(σ*ᵢ)

Condition (1) is the equaliser you solve. Condition (2) says nothing outside the support does better — and it is trivially satisfied when the support is the whole strategy set, which is why 2 × 2 fully-mixed problems only need (1). For anything with an unused strategy, condition (2) is a real check and skipping it loses marks.

The direction that trips people

Player 1's probabilities are pinned down by making player 2 indifferent, and vice versa. Your own payoffs never appear in your own equation. Say it once at the top of your answer — "solving for p from player 2's indifference" — and the marker can follow you even if the arithmetic slips.

Matching pennies, both directions

let player B play H with probability q U_A(H) = q(1) + (1−q)(−1) = 2q − 1 U_A(T) = q(−1) + (1−q)(1) = 1 − 2q Indifference: 2q − 1 = 1 − 2q ⇒ 4q = 2 ⇒ q = ½ Symmetrically p = ½. Equilibrium payoffs U_A = U_B = 0.

Check what indifference bought: at q = ½, any mixture by A is a best reply, because U_A(σ_A) = p·0 + (1−p)·0 = 0 regardless of p. That is the whole logic of mixing — you are not optimising, you are being made indifferent, and the specific value of p is fixed only by the requirement that B be indifferent too.

5.3 The 2 × 2 case, in full

Battle of the sexes, the standard worked example. Let σ*₁(A) = x, σ*₂(A) = y, both strictly between 0 and 1 so the support is {A,B} × {A,B}.

u: (2,1) (0,0) / (0,0) (1,2) Player 1's payoffs, given y: u₁(A, σ*₂) = y(2) + (1−y)(0) = 2y u₁(B, σ*₂) = y(0) + (1−y)(1) = 1 − y Condition (1): 2y = 1 − y ⇒ 3y = 1 ⇒ y = 1/3 Player 2's payoffs, given x: u₂(σ*₁, A) = x(1) + (1−x)(0) = x u₂(σ*₁, B) = x(0) + (1−x)(2) = 2(1 − x) Condition (1): x = 2 − 2x ⇒ 3x = 2 ⇒ x = 2/3 MSNE: σ*₁ = (2/3, 1/3), σ*₂ = (1/3, 2/3) Payoffs: u₁ = 2(1/3) = 2/3, u₂ = 2/3.
Sanity checks worth 30 seconds
  • Both probabilities strictly inside (0, 1)? If one comes out negative or above 1, that support is not an equilibrium — report that and move to a different support.
  • Substitute back: both of player 1's pure payoffs should be equal, and both of player 2's should be equal.
  • Compare with the pure equilibria. In BoS the mixed payoff 2/3 is worse for both than either PSNE — a standard follow-up question.
Lab 5 · 2 × 2 mixed equilibrium, step by step

5.4 Oddments — the zero-sum shortcut

For a 2 × 2 zero-sum game with no saddle point there is a mechanical formula. With payoffs to Rose:

the oddment rule Colin A Colin B Rose oddment Rose A a b |d − c| Rose B c d |a − b| Colin oddment |d − b| |a − c| Rose plays A with probability (d − c) / [(a − b) + (d − c)] Colin plays A with probability (d − b) / [(a − c) + (d − b)] Value v = (ad − bc) / [(a + d) − (b + c)]

Rose’s oddments use differences across rows; Colin’s use differences down columns. Deriving indifference equations avoids mixing up the two. Worked on the slides' example [2, −3 ; 0, 3]:

a=2, b=−3, c=0, d=3 Rose: (3 − 0) / [(2 − (−3)) + (3 − 0)] = 3/8 → Rose (3/8 A, 5/8 B) Colin: (3 − (−3)) / [(2 − 0) + (3 − (−3))] = 6/8 → Colin (3/4 A, 1/4 B) v = (2·3 − (−3)·0) / [(2 + 3) − (−3 + 0)] = 6/8 = 3/4 Verify by equalising: Colin plays A with prob x. Rose A: 2x − 3(1−x) = 5x − 3 Rose B: 0x + 3(1−x) = 3 − 3x 5x − 3 = 3 − 3x ⇒ 8x = 6 ⇒ x = 3/4 ✓ and v = 5(3/4) − 3 = 3/4 ✓
Failure mode

Applying oddments when a saddle point exists. The denominator can vanish or the "probabilities" can leave [0,1]. Always check for a saddle point first — maxmin against minmax — and only mix if they differ.

Lab 6 · Oddments calculator (2 × 2 zero-sum)

5.5 The graphical method for 2 × n and m × 2

In one line

A 2 × n zero-sum game without a saddle point always reduces to one of its 2 × 2 subgames, and the graph tells you which one without trying them all.

m × 2 — Colin has two strategies, mixing x on B 1. Horizontal axis: x from 0 (Colin plays A) to 1 (Colin plays B). 2. For each ROSE strategy draw the line from its payoff-vs-A on the left axis to its payoff-vs-B on the right axis. 3. Rose picks her best reply, so she rides the UPPER ENVELOPE. 4. Colin picks x to hold Rose down: the LOWEST POINT of the upper envelope. 5. The two lines crossing there name the active 2 × 2 subgame. Solve it. For 2 × n (Rose has two strategies) flip every rule: draw one line per COLIN strategy, Colin rides the LOWER ENVELOPE, Rose picks the HIGHEST POINT on it.

[2, −3 ; 0, 2] Rose = (2/7, 5/7, 0) Colin = (5/7, 2/7) value = 4/7 Verify — Rose's expectations against Colin (5/7, 2/7): A: (5/7)(2) + (2/7)(−3) = 4/7 B: (5/7)(0) + (2/7)(2) = 4/7 C: (5/7)(−5) + (2/7)(10) = −5/7 ← strictly below v, so C is correctly unused Colin's expectations against Rose (2/7, 5/7, 0): A: (2/7)(2) + (5/7)(0) = 4/7 B: (2/7)(−3) + (5/7)(2) = 4/7 All Rose's ≤ 4/7 and all Colin's ≥ 4/7 ⇒ value confirmed = 4/7.

Lab 7 · Graphical solver — envelopes and the active subgame

5.6 Equalising expectations on a 3 × 3

When the solution uses all strategies you can equalise directly, without graphs. Take the zero-sum game below, which has no saddle point.

Rose \ ColinABC
A122
B212
C220
let Colin play (x, y, 1 − x − y) Rose A: x(1) + y(2) + (1−x−y)(2) = 2 − x Rose B: x(2) + y(1) + (1−x−y)(2) = 2 − y Rose C: x(2) + y(2) + (1−x−y)(0) = 2x + 2y Set all three equal: 2 − x = 2 − y ⇒ x = y 2 − x = 2x + 2y = 4x ⇒ 2 = 5x ⇒ x = 2/5 Colin = (2/5, 2/5, 1/5). Here direct substitution also gives pᵀA = (8/5, 8/5, 8/5) for p = (2/5, 2/5, 1/5), so Rose uses this mixture too. The matrix is symmetric under transpose, not transpose-and-negate. Value = 2 − 2/5 = 8/5.
When equalising fails

If the true solution uses only a 2 × 2 or 1 × 1 subgame, forcing all three expectations equal gives a probability outside [0,1] or an inconsistent system. So: check for a saddle point, then for dominance, then try equalising. If equalising fails, fall back to the graphical analysis of the three 2 × 3 subgames.

5.7 Support enumeration — finding all equilibria

"Find all Nash equilibria" means: every pure one, and every mixed one, and a statement that nothing else exists. The systematic method is to work through the possible supports.

the procedure 1. Find all PSNE. These are the equilibria with singleton supports. 2. For every other pair of supports (δ₁, δ₂): write the indifference equations from condition (1), solve for the probabilities, REJECT if any probability falls outside (0, 1), REJECT if condition (2) fails for a strategy outside a support. 3. Report the survivors. State that the list is exhaustive.

BoS, done exhaustively

Each player has three possible supports — {A}, {B}, {A,B} — so nine support pairs.

δ(σ₁) × δ(σ₂)Outcome
{A} × {A}Equilibrium — the PSNE (A, A), payoffs (2, 1)
{B} × {B}Equilibrium — the PSNE (B, B), payoffs (1, 2)
{A,B} × {A,B}Equilibrium — x = 2/3, y = 1/3, payoffs (2/3, 2/3)
{A} × {B}, {B} × {A}Fail — neither is a mutual best reply, payoffs (0,0)
{A} × {A,B}Fail — if 1 surely plays A, player 2 strictly prefers A, so 2 cannot mix
{B} × {A,B}Fail — if 1 surely plays B, player 2 strictly prefers B
{A,B} × {A}Fail — if 2 surely plays A, player 1 strictly prefers A
{A,B} × {B}Fail — if 2 surely plays B, player 1 strictly prefers B

So BoS has exactly three equilibria. The pattern generalises: a mixed support for one player requires the other's mixture to make them indifferent, which is impossible when the other is playing a pure strategy that breaks the tie.

A useful counting fact

Almost every finite game has an odd number of equilibria. Two PSNE in a 2 × 2 coordination-type game therefore all but guarantees a third, mixed one — worth remembering as a check that you have not stopped early.

Lab 8 · Support enumeration — every equilibrium

5.8 Security values in mixed strategies

Sheet, Definitions 23–24 v̲ᵢ = max(σᵢ ∈ Δ(Sᵢ)) min(σ₋ᵢ) uᵢ(σᵢ, σ₋ᵢ) v̄ᵢ = min(σ₋ᵢ) max(σᵢ ∈ Δ(Sᵢ)) uᵢ(σᵢ, σ₋ᵢ) Payoff at any MSNE ≥ v̲ᵢ, the mixed maxmin value.

Allowing mixtures can only raise the maxmin value, because the pure strategies are still available as degenerate mixtures. In the matching pennies game the pure maxmin is −1 — whatever you pick, the opponent can beat it — but the mixed maxmin is 0, achieved by (½, ½). That gap is exactly what the minimax theorem closes for zero-sum games: with mixing allowed, v̲ᵢ = v̄ᵢ always, and the common value is the value of the game.

Dominance among mixed strategies

Definitions 25–26 lift the three grades to mixtures unchanged: σᵢ strictly dominates σ′ᵢ if uᵢ(σᵢ, σ₋ᵢ) > uᵢ(σ′ᵢ, σ₋ᵢ) for every σ₋ᵢ. Any dominant mixed strategy equilibrium is a mixed Nash equilibrium, and a strictly dominant mixed strategy, if one exists, is unique.

check

Solve (0,0) (7,2) / (2,7) (6,6) — the game of chicken — completely.

PSNE at (D, C) → (7,2) and (C, D) → (2,7). For the mixed one, let player 1 play D with probability p; player 2 is indifferent when 2p + 6(1−p) = 0p + 7(1−p), i.e. 6 − 4p = 7 − 7p, so 3p = 1, p = 1/3. By symmetry q = 1/3. Equilibrium payoffs 14/3 ≈ 4.67 each — worse for both than the (6,6) they could have had by both swerving, and that is the point of the game.

A 2 × 2 game has a strictly dominant strategy for player 1. Can it have a fully mixed equilibrium?

No. Player 1 would have to be indifferent between two strategies, but strict dominance makes one strictly better against every mixture of player 2. The only equilibria put probability 1 on the dominant strategy.

Why is the equilibrium probability sometimes negative when you solve the equations?

Because you assumed the wrong support. A negative or above-one "probability" is the algebra telling you that no equilibrium exists with those strategies both played. Reject that support and try another.

Sheet: Definitions 18–26, Theorems 1–2, Proposition 1. Slides: Mixed Strategy Nash Equilibrium.

Part 06

Correlated equilibrium

Drop the independence assumption, add a mediator, and some games admit payoff improvements beyond their Nash payoff set.

nash assumes independent randomisation. correlated equilibrium is what you get when you stop assuming it.

one constraint per (recommended sᵢ, deviation s′ᵢ) pair, per player. count them before you start.

every NE is a CE. the reverse is false, and that gap is the whole point.

6.1 Correlated strategies and the mediator

In one line

A mediator draws one cell of the matrix from a public distribution, whispers each player only their own coordinate, and the distribution is a correlated equilibrium if nobody ever wants to disobey their whisper.

Sheet, Definitions 27–28 A correlated strategy for a coalition C ⊆ N is a probability distribution over ×(i∈C) Sᵢ — a joint distribution, not a product of independent ones. A contract τ = (τ_C)(C ⊆ N) ∈ ×(C⊆N) Δ(×(i∈C) Sᵢ) is a vector of correlated strategies, one for every possible coalition.

The contrast with a mixed strategy profile is the whole idea. A mixed profile (σ₁, σ₂) induces the product distribution σ₁(s₁)·σ₂(s₂) over cells. A correlated strategy α ∈ Δ(S₁ × S₂) is any distribution at all — including ones no independent pair could produce, such as "1/2 on (A,A) and 1/2 on (B,B), nothing elsewhere".

Individual rationality

Sheet, Definition 29 Security level: v̲ᵢ = max(τᵢ ∈ Δ(Sᵢ)) min(s_{N−i}) uᵢ(τᵢ, s_{N−i}) uᵢ(τᵢ, s_{N−i}) = Σ(sᵢ ∈ Sᵢ) τᵢ(sᵢ) uᵢ(sᵢ, s_{N−i}) α ∈ Δ(S₁ × ⋯ × Sₙ) is individually rational ⟺ uᵢ(α) ≥ v̲ᵢ ∀ i ∈ N.

Two propositions from the sheet close the loop on the contract-signing game. Given any individually rational α there is a contract τ with τ_N = α such that everyone signing is a Nash equilibrium of the signing game; and conversely, at any Nash equilibrium of a contract-signing game induced by α, every player gets at least their security level. Individual rationality is exactly the condition for a contract to be signable.

6.2 The strategic incentive constraints

Sheet, Definition 30 and its working form α ∈ Δ(S) is a CORRELATED EQUILIBRIUM if, for every deviation map δᵢ : Sᵢ → Sᵢ, uᵢ(α) ≥ Σ((sᵢ,s₋ᵢ) ∈ S) α(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ) · uᵢ(δᵢ(sᵢ), s₋ᵢ) ∀ i ∈ N which is EQUIVALENT to the pairwise form you actually compute with: Σ(s₋ᵢ ∈ S₋ᵢ) α(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ) · [ uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ) − uᵢ(s′ᵢ, s₋ᵢ) ] ≥ 0 ∀ sᵢ ∈ Sᵢ, ∀ s′ᵢ ∈ Sᵢ, ∀ i ∈ N

Read the working form in words: given that I was told to play sᵢ, my conditional expected gain from obeying rather than switching to s′ᵢ is non-negative. These are the strategic incentive constraints. For a two-player game with |S₁| = m, |S₂| = n there are m(m−1) + n(n−1) of them — for 2 × 2, exactly four.

Why the α-weighting is there and not a division

The true condition is about conditional expectations given the recommendation, which would need α(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ)/α(sᵢ). Multiplying through by the positive constant α(sᵢ) clears the denominator and gives the linear form above. That linearity is what makes the set of correlated equilibria a polytope — computable by linear programming, unlike the Nash equilibrium set.

Worked: battle of the sexes

Take α putting 1/2 on (A,A) and 1/2 on (B,B) — a fair coin the mediator tosses in public, telling each player where to go.

u: (2,1) (0,0) / (0,0) (1,2) — four constraints P1 told A, considers B: α(A,A)[u₁(A,A) − u₁(B,A)] + α(A,B)[u₁(A,B) − u₁(B,B)] = ½[2 − 0] + 0[0 − 1] = 1 ≥ 0 ✓ P1 told B, considers A: α(B,A)[u₁(B,A) − u₁(A,A)] + α(B,B)[u₁(B,B) − u₁(A,B)] = 0[0 − 2] + ½[1 − 0] = ½ ≥ 0 ✓ P2 told A, considers B: α(A,A)[u₂(A,A) − u₂(A,B)] + α(B,A)[u₂(B,A) − u₂(B,B)] = ½[1 − 0] + 0[0 − 2] = ½ ≥ 0 ✓ P2 told B, considers A: α(A,B)[u₂(A,B) − u₂(A,A)] + α(B,B)[u₂(B,B) − u₂(B,A)] = 0[0 − 1] + ½[2 − 0] = 1 ≥ 0 ✓ All four hold ⇒ correlated equilibrium. Payoffs = ½(2,1) + ½(1,2) = (1.5, 1.5). Compare: MSNE gives (2/3, 2/3). Both players strictly better off.

The mechanism is intuitive once you see it. Told "A", player 1 knows player 2 was told "A" too, so deviating to B earns 0 instead of 2. The correlation destroys the miscoordination risk that made the mixed equilibrium so poor.

6.3 Payoffs beyond the Nash payoff hull

Chicken is the sharper example, because the correlated equilibrium payoff lies strictly outside the convex hull of the Nash payoffs.

1 \ 2DareChicken
Dare0, 07, 2
Chicken2, 76, 6
α = 1/3 each on (D,C), (C,D), (C,C); zero on (D,D) Every one of the four strategic incentive constraints evaluates to 1/3 ≥ 0. ✓ Payoffs: ⅓(7,2) + ⅓(2,7) + ⅓(6,6) = (5, 5). For comparison in this game: PSNE (D,C) = (7,2) and (C,D) = (2,7) MSNE p(D) = q(D) = 1/3, payoffs (14/3, 14/3) ≈ (4.67, 4.67) (5,5) beats the mixed equilibrium for both, and is not a mixture of the two pure ones.
The containment to state in an answer

Every Nash equilibrium is a correlated equilibrium — take α to be the product distribution Π σᵢ(sᵢ) and the constraints follow from the Nash best-response inequalities (with indifference on any mixed support). The converse fails, as chicken shows. So NE ⊆ CE, strictly.

Lab 9 · Correlated equilibrium checker
check

How many strategic incentive constraints does a 3 × 3 two-player game have?

3(3−1) + 3(3−1) = 12 — six per player, one for each ordered pair of distinct strategies.

In the prisoner's dilemma, can a mediator do better than (C, C)?

No. Defection strictly dominates, so the constraint for "told NC, considers C" fails for any α putting weight on an NC cell. The unique correlated equilibrium is the point mass on (C, C). Correlation only helps when there is coordination value to capture.

Why is the set of correlated equilibria always non-empty?

Every finite game has at least one mixed Nash equilibrium, and the induced product distribution is a correlated equilibrium. The set is also convex and compact, being the solution set of finitely many linear inequalities.

Sheet: Definitions 27–30, Propositions 2–3.

Part 07

Two-person bargaining

A feasible set, a disagreement point, and one maximisation that Nash's axioms make unique.

the Nash bargaining solution is just argmax of a product. everything else is justification.

v is the payoff if talks collapse. it is always inside F.

maximise (x₁−v₁)(x₂−v₂), not x₁x₂. forgetting v is the standard slip.

7.1 The problem (F, v)

In one line

Two players can reach any payoff pair in a closed convex set F; if they fail to agree they get v; the question is which point of F they should settle on.

ObjectRequirementMeaning
F ⊆ ℝ²closed and convexthe feasible payoff allocations. Convex because they can randomise between deals
v = (v₁, v₂)always chosen inside Fthe disagreement / status-quo / default point
F ∩ {x : x₁ ≥ v₁, x₂ ≥ v₂}non-empty and boundedthere is something to gain, and gains are finite

A problem is essential when that intersection contains a point strictly better than v for both. Without a feasible strict gain for both players, the standard positive-gains uniqueness argument does not apply; state the convention used for the nonessential case.

7.2 The Nash bargaining solution

Sheet, Theorem 3 f(F, v) ∈ argmax((x₁,x₂) ∈ F) (x₁ − v₁)(x₂ − v₂) subject to x₁ ≥ v₁, x₂ ≥ v₂ The maximand (x₁ − v₁)(x₂ − v₂) is the NASH PRODUCT. The standard axioms (invariance to positive affine rescaling, Pareto efficiency, symmetry, independence of irrelevant alternatives) make f unique.
The procedure, every time
  1. Write the efficient frontier of F as an equation. If F is "split 100", that is x₁ + x₂ = 100.
  2. Substitute the frontier into the Nash product to get one variable.
  3. Differentiate, set to zero, solve. Check the endpoint constraints xᵢ ≥ vᵢ.

Worked: splitting 100 with a linear frontier

F = {x₁ + x₂ ≤ 100, x ≥ 0} Frontier x₂ = 100 − x₁. Maximise g(x₁) = (x₁ − v₁)(100 − x₁ − v₂). g′(x₁) = (100 − x₁ − v₂) − (x₁ − v₁) = 0 ⇒ x₁ = (100 + v₁ − v₂) / 2 , x₂ = (100 − v₁ + v₂) / 2 v = (0, 0) → (50, 50) product 2500 v = (20, 0) → (60, 40) product 1600 v = (20, 10) → (55, 45) product 1225

The structure is worth stating in words because it is the interpretation questions ask for: each player receives their disagreement payoff, and then the surplus is split equally. With v = (20, 0) the surplus is 100 − 20 = 80, split 40/40, giving (60, 40). With this fixed total, increasing one outside option by one unit raises that player’s allocation by one-half unit, holding the other outside option fixed.

Worked: a tilted frontier

F bounded by 2x₁ + x₂ = 20, v = (0,0) x₂ = 20 − 2x₁ , maximise x₁(20 − 2x₁) = 20x₁ − 2x₁² derivative 20 − 4x₁ = 0 ⇒ x₁ = 5, x₂ = 10, Nash product 50. Note the split is NOT equal in payoff units — player 2's payoffs are "cheaper" to produce, so player 2 gets more of them. The weighted gains are equal here: 2x₁ = x₂ = 10. Unweighted gains need not be equal on a tilted frontier.

The λ characterisation

Sheet, Proposition 4 — for an essential problem, x* ∈ F with x* ≥ v x* is the Nash bargaining solution ⟺ ∃ λ₁, λ₂ > 0 with λ₁x*₁ − λ₁v₁ = λ₂x*₂ − λ₂v₂ (equal weighted surplus) λ₁x*₁ + λ₂x*₂ = max(y ∈ F) (λ₁y₁ + λ₂y₂) (supporting line)

Geometrically: the line λ₁x₁ + λ₂x₂ = const through x* supports F, and the tangency is exactly where a hyperbola (x₁−v₁)(x₂−v₂) = k touches the frontier. Checking the two λ conditions is the standard way a question asks you to verify a proposed solution rather than derive one.

Lab 10 · Nash bargaining solution
check

Two firms split a surplus of 60. Firm 1's outside option is 10, firm 2's is 20. Nash bargaining solution?

Surplus after outside options is 60 − 10 − 20 = 30, split equally at 15 each. So x = (25, 35). Check: 25 + 35 = 60 and (25−10)(35−20) = 15 × 15 = 225, and any other split on the frontier gives less.

Player 1's disagreement payoff improves from 0 to 10 while the frontier x₁ + x₂ = 100 is unchanged. What happens?

Player 1 moves from 50 to 55, player 2 from 50 to 45. Half the improvement in the outside option converts to bargaining gain.

Why must F be convex?

Players can agree to randomise between two deals, so any convex combination of feasible payoff pairs must itself be feasible. In an essential problem with a bounded individually rational region, strict concavity of the log of the Nash product on positive gains gives uniqueness over the convex feasible region.

Sheet: Theorem 3, Proposition 4.

Part 08

Coalitional games

The switch from "what does each player do" to "what is each group worth".

no strategies here. just v(C) for every subset, and how to divide v(N).

v(∅) = 0, always. it is part of the definition, and it matters in the Shapley sum.

superadditive is about DISJOINT coalitions. convex is about all pairs. convex ⟹ superadditive.

8.1 TU and NTU games

Sheet, Definitions 31–32 TU game: (N, v) with v : 2^N → ℝ, v(∅) = 0. "transferable utility" — the coalition's worth is one number, freely divisible. Also called a game in coalition form / characteristic form. NTU game: (N, V) with V(C) a non-empty closed convex subset of ℝ^|C|, and { x ∈ V(C) : xᵢ ≥ vᵢ ∀ i ∈ C } bounded, where vᵢ = max{ yᵢ : y ∈ V({i}) }. Used when payoffs cannot be transferred one-for-one.

For n players there are 2ⁿ coalitions including ∅, so a 3-player game needs 8 numbers of which v(∅) = 0 is fixed. Questions are almost always TU and almost always n = 3 or a small weighted voting game.

8.2 Imputations and domination

Sheet, Definitions 33–34 x = (x₁,…,xₙ) is an IMPUTATION if individual rationality: xᵢ ≥ v({i}) ∀ i ∈ N collective rationality: Σ(i∈N) xᵢ = v(N) x dominates y via coalition C (written x ≻_C y) if Σ(i∈C) xᵢ ≤ v(C) (C can actually afford x) and xᵢ > yᵢ ∀ i ∈ C (every member of C strictly prefers x)

An imputation is the minimum bar for a sensible payoff division: nobody accepts less than they could get alone, and nothing is left on the table. Domination is a strictly stronger objection than "some player prefers x" — the whole coalition must prefer it and be able to deliver it.

8.3 Special structures

PropertyConditionHow to check quickly
Monotonicv(C) ≤ v(D) ∀ C ⊆ D ⊆ NAdding members never reduces worth. Check each cover relation
Superadditivev(C ∪ D) ≥ v(C) + v(D) for disjoint C, DMerging disjoint groups never hurts. Only disjoint pairs
InessentialΣᵢ v({i}) = v(N)Nothing is gained by cooperating; otherwise essential
Convexv(C ∪ D) + v(C ∩ D) ≥ v(C) + v(D) ∀ C, DMarginal contributions grow with coalition size. Convex ⟹ superadditive
Strategically equivalentw(C) = b(v(C) + Σi∈C cᵢ), b > 0Rescale all payoffs and shift each player by a constant
The distinction that gets tested

Superadditivity quantifies over disjoint pairs only. Convexity quantifies over all pairs and, applied to disjoint C, D, gives v(C∪D) + v(∅) ≥ v(C) + v(D) — superadditivity. So convex is strictly stronger. A game can be superadditive and not convex, and that is exactly the case where the core is non-empty but the Shapley value falls outside it.

Worked: checking a 3-player game

v(1)=v(2)=v(3)=0, v(12)=90, v(13)=80, v(23)=70, v(123)=120 Monotonic? 0 ≤ 70,80,90 ≤ 120 everywhere. ✓ Superadditive? v(12) = 90 ≥ v(1)+v(2) = 0 ✓ (same for 13, 23) v(123) = 120 ≥ v(12)+v(3) = 90 ✓, ≥ v(13)+v(2) = 80 ✓, ≥ v(23)+v(1) = 70 ✓ → superadditive ✓ Essential? Σ v({i}) = 0 ≠ 120 = v(N) → essential ✓ Convex? Take C = {1,2}, D = {1,3}: C∪D = {1,2,3}, C∩D = {1} v(C∪D) + v(C∩D) = 120 + 0 = 120 v(C) + v(D) = 90 + 80 = 170 120 < 170 → NOT convex ✗
check

Is v(C) = |C|² on N = {1,2,3} convex?

Yes. Check the definition on C = {1,2}, D = {2,3}: v(123) + v(2) = 9 + 1 = 10 ≥ v(12) + v(23) = 4 + 4 = 8. The pattern holds generally because |C∪D|² + |C∩D|² ≥ |C|² + |D|² whenever |C∪D| + |C∩D| = |C| + |D| and the squares are convex.

A game has v({i}) = 5 for all three players and v(N) = 15. Essential?

No — Σ v({i}) = 15 = v(N), so it is inessential. There is no surplus from cooperating and the only imputation is (5,5,5).

Sheet: Definitions 31–40.

Part 09

The core

The set of divisions no coalition can walk away from. Often empty, sometimes a single point.

core = one equation (Σ over N) plus one inequality per coalition. write them all out.

shortcut for 3 players: Σx = v(N) turns "x₁ + x₂ ≥ v(12)" into "x₃ ≤ v(N) − v(12)".

if the three upper bounds sum to less than v(N), the core is EMPTY. that check takes ten seconds.

9.1 The definition, and the four rationalities

Sheet, Definitions 41–44 feasible for C: Σ(i∈C) xᵢ ≤ v(C) individually rational: xᵢ ≥ v({i}) ∀ i ∈ N collectively rational: Σ(i∈N) xᵢ = v(N) coalitionally rational: Σ(i∈C) xᵢ ≥ v(C) ∀ C ⊆ N C(N, v) = { x ∈ ℝⁿ : Σ(i∈N) xᵢ = v(N) and Σ(i∈C) xᵢ ≥ v(C) ∀ C ⊆ N }

Coalitional rationality with C = {i} gives individual rationality, so the core is automatically a set of imputations. For strict blocking, use the following correction to the sheet’s weak inequality: coalition C blocks (or "can improve on") x when v(C) > Σ_{i∈C} xᵢ, and the core is precisely the set of feasible allocations no coalition blocks.

The three-player shortcut

With x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = v(N), every two-player constraint converts into a ceiling on the excluded player:

x₁ + x₂ ≥ v(12) ⟺ x₃ ≤ v(N) − v(12) x₁ + x₃ ≥ v(13) ⟺ x₂ ≤ v(N) − v(13) x₂ + x₃ ≥ v(23) ⟺ x₁ ≤ v(N) − v(23)

So the core of a 3-player game is a box v({i}) ≤ xᵢ ≤ v(N) − v(N∖{i}) intersected with the plane Σ xᵢ = v(N). The exact feasibility test is: every floor Lᵢ ≤ its ceiling Uᵢ, and ΣLᵢ ≤ v(N) ≤ ΣUᵢ. A ceiling sum below v(N) proves emptiness, but a larger sum alone does not prove feasibility.

Worked: a core that collapses to a point

v(1)=v(2)=v(3)=0, v(12)=90, v(13)=80, v(23)=70, v(123)=120 Ceilings: x₃ ≤ 120 − 90 = 30 x₂ ≤ 120 − 80 = 40 x₁ ≤ 120 − 70 = 50 Sum of ceilings = 30 + 40 + 50 = 120 = v(N), exactly. The ceilings sum to precisely v(N), so every one must bind: CORE = { (50, 40, 30) } — a single point. Floors xᵢ ≥ 0 are satisfied, so the core is non-empty.
Failure mode

If the ceilings had summed to less than v(N) the core would be empty — the constraints cannot all be met while still distributing v(N). If they sum to more, also check the floors and each floor–ceiling pair. A feasible core may be a point, segment, or polygon; identify vertices to determine its shape.

Lab 11 · Core and Shapley value for a 3-player TU game

9.2 When is the core non-empty?

Sheet, Definition 47 and Theorem 5 — Bondareva–Shapley (N, v) is BALANCED if, whenever weights α(C) ≥ 0 satisfy Σ(C ⊇ {i}) α(C) = 1 for every i ∈ N (a balanced family) it follows that Σ(C ⊆ N) α(C) v(C) ≤ v(N). Theorem: the core of (N, v) is non-empty ⟺ (N, v) is balanced.

The linear program behind it, also on the sheet: minimise x₁ + ⋯ + xₙ subject to Σ_{i∈C} xᵢ ≥ v(C) for all C. This finds the cheapest allocation no coalition can improve on; the core is non-empty exactly when the optimum is at most v(N). Balancedness is the dual condition.

The standard empty-core example

simple majority: v(C) = 1 if |C| ≥ 2, else 0; v(N) = 1 Ceilings: xᵢ ≤ v(N) − v(N∖{i}) = 1 − 1 = 0 for every i. So x₁ = x₂ = x₃ = 0, but then Σ xᵢ = 0 ≠ 1 = v(N). CORE IS EMPTY. Balancedness fails with α({1,2}) = α({1,3}) = α({2,3}) = ½ : each player is in exactly two of those coalitions, ½ + ½ = 1 ✓ balanced family Σ α(C)v(C) = ½ + ½ + ½ = 3/2 > 1 = v(N) ✗

9.3 The core of a convex game

Sheet, Proposition 5 For a CONVEX game (N, v), the marginal-contribution vector along any ordering lies in the core. For the ordering 1, 2, …, n: x₁ = v({1}) x₂ = v({1,2}) − v({1}) ⋮ xₙ = v({1,…,n}) − v({1,…,n−1}) Then x ∈ C(N, v). In particular the core of a convex game is never empty, and the Shapley value — an average of these vectors — is inside it.

Take the convex game v(1)=v(2)=v(3)=0, v(12)=4, v(13)=3, v(23)=2, v(123)=9. The ordering 1, 2, 3 gives x = (0, 4, 5), and every one of the six orderings produces a different core point. Their average is the Shapley value (7/2, 3, 5/2), which is therefore also in the core — a convenient way to answer "is the Shapley value in the core" without checking each constraint.

The three-way summary to memorise
  • Convex ⟹ core non-empty and Shapley value in the core.
  • Balanced ⟺ core non-empty. Superadditive alone guarantees neither.
  • Core can be empty, a point, or a polytope. Shapley value always exists and is always unique.
check

v(1)=v(2)=v(3)=0, v(12)=60, v(13)=60, v(23)=60, v(123)=90. Is the core empty?

Ceilings xᵢ ≤ 90 − 60 = 30 each, summing to 90 = v(N). So the core is the single point (30, 30, 30) — non-empty.

Same game but v(123) = 80. Now?

Ceilings are 80 − 60 = 20 each, summing to 60 < 80. Empty core: no way to distribute 80 while keeping every pair at 60 or more.

Why is the core of a convex game always non-empty without checking balancedness?

Proposition 5 exhibits a core element directly — the marginal-contribution vector along any ordering. An explicit member is enough.

Sheet: Definitions 41–47, Theorems 4–5, Proposition 5.

Part 10

Shapley value and power indices

One formula, three names, and an arithmetic routine you should be able to run in ninety seconds.

for n = 3 the weights are only 1/3, 1/6, 1/6, 1/3. write that row down first.

easier route: average the marginal contribution over all n! orderings. same answer, less factorial arithmetic.

check Σφᵢ = v(N). if it does not, you dropped a term.

10.1 The formula and how to run it

Sheet, Theorem 6 — Shapley's theorem φᵢ(v) = Σ(C ⊆ N∖{i}) [ |C|! (|N| − |C| − 1)! / |N|! ] · [ v(C ∪ {i}) − v(C) ]

Two readings of the same object. The formula sums over subsets not containing i, weighting each marginal contribution. The ordering reading: line the players up in one of n! random orders, give each their marginal contribution to whoever is already in, and average. The bracket is exactly the probability that C is the set of players ahead of i.

The n = 3 weight table — write this first
C|C|weight |C|!(2−|C|)!/6
∅00!·2!/6 = 2/6 = 1/3
one other player11!·1!/6 = 1/6 (each of the two)
both others22!·0!/6 = 2/6 = 1/3

The weights sum to 1/3 + 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/3 = 1, which is the check that you have all four terms.

Worked, both ways

Game: v(1)=v(2)=v(3)=0, v(12)=90, v(13)=80, v(23)=70, v(123)=120.

by the formula, player 1 C = ∅ w = 1/3 v(1) − v(∅) = 0 − 0 = 0 → 0 C = {2} w = 1/6 v(12) − v(2) = 90 − 0 = 90 → 15 C = {3} w = 1/6 v(13) − v(3) = 80 − 0 = 80 → 40/3 C = {2,3} w = 1/3 v(123) − v(23) = 120 − 70 = 50 → 50/3 φ₁ = 0 + 15 + 40/3 + 50/3 = 15 + 90/3 = 15 + 30 = 45
by orderings — six rows, marginal contributions order player 1 player 2 player 3 1 2 3 v(1)=0 v(12)−v(1)=90 v(123)−v(12)=30 1 3 2 v(1)=0 v(123)−v(13)=40 v(13)−v(1)=80 2 1 3 v(12)−v(2)=90 v(2)=0 v(123)−v(12)=30 2 3 1 v(123)−v(23)=50 v(2)=0 v(23)−v(2)=70 3 1 2 v(13)−v(3)=80 v(123)−v(13)=40 v(3)=0 3 2 1 v(123)−v(23)=50 v(23)−v(3)=70 v(3)=0 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── sums 270 240 210 ÷ 6 45 40 35 ✓ sums to 120 = v(N)
The follow-up they will ask

The core of this game is the single point (50, 40, 30) — see §9.1 — and the Shapley value is (45, 40, 35). So the Shapley value is not in the core: coalition {1,2} gets 45 + 40 = 85 < 90 = v(12) and would block. This is not an error; it is the standard demonstration that fairness and stability are different criteria. The game is superadditive but not convex, so this outcome is possible; non-convexity does not force the Shapley value outside the core.

10.2 Shapley–Shubik and Banzhaf

Applied to a simple game — v(C) ∈ {0, 1}, coalitions either win or lose — the Shapley value becomes a power index. A weighted voting game is written [q; w₁,…,wₙ]: coalition C wins iff Σ_{i∈C} wᵢ ≥ q.

Sheet Shapley–Shubik: φᵢ(v) = Σ(C ∈ Qᵢ(N,v)) |C|! (n − |C| − 1)! / n! where Qᵢ is the set of coalitions C ⊆ N∖{i} that LOSE but where C ∪ {i} WINS. Equivalently: the fraction of the n! orderings in which i is PIVOTAL. Banzhaf: ψᵢ(N, v) = (1 / 2^{n−1}) Σ(C ⊆ N∖{i}) [ v(C ∪ {i}) − v(C) ] Counts SWINGS — coalitions i turns from losing to winning — over all 2^{n−1} subsets of the others, each weighted equally.
The difference in one sentence

Shapley–Shubik weights by orderings (so coalition size matters); Banzhaf weights by subsets (so every coalition of others counts the same). Absolute Banzhaf values need not sum to 1; the normalised Banzhaf index divides each by their total.

Worked: [51; 40, 30, 30]

winning coalitions: {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3}, {1,2,3} Every two-player coalition wins; no single player wins. Each player is pivotal in exactly 2 of the 6 orderings → Shapley–Shubik = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). Banzhaf swings for player 1: C = {2} (lose→win) ✓, C = {3} ✓, C = ∅ ✗, C = {2,3} ✗ ψ₁ = 2/4 = 1/2, same for 2 and 3. Normalised: (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). The 40-vote player has NO more power than the 30-vote players. Weights are not power.

Worked: [51; 49, 48, 3]

the classic {1,2} = 97 ✓ {1,3} = 52 ✓ {2,3} = 51 ✓ any singleton ✗ Structurally identical to [51; 40,30,30] — every pair wins, no singleton does. Shapley–Shubik = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). The tiny 3-vote party has equal power.

Worked: [51; 50, 49, 1] — a veto player

winning: {1,2}, {1,3}, {1,2,3} Player 1 is in every winning coalition — a VETO player. Shapley–Shubik = (2/3, 1/6, 1/6). Banzhaf raw = (3/4, 1/4, 1/4); normalised = (3/5, 1/5, 1/5). Note the two indices DISAGREE here — a standard "compare the two" question.
Lab 12 · Voting power — Shapley–Shubik and Banzhaf
check

In [51; 40, 30, 20, 10], which players are dummies?

None, but player 4 is nearly one: their Shapley–Shubik index is 1/12 while players 2 and 3 each hold 1/4 and player 1 holds 5/12. A true dummy has index 0, which happens when they are never pivotal — check by seeing whether removing them ever changes a coalition's winning status.

What does Σᵢ φᵢ(v) = v(N) correspond to in a voting game?

The Shapley–Shubik indices sum to 1, since v(N) = 1 for a simple game where the grand coalition wins. It is the efficiency axiom, and it is your arithmetic check.

Compute the Shapley value of v(1)=v(2)=v(3)=0, v(12)=v(13)=v(23)=v(123)=1.

Symmetric, so (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). Its core is empty (see §9.2), so this is a case where the Shapley value exists but no stable allocation does.

Part 11

Mechanism design — the setting

The last block on the sheet. The vocabulary sets up the problem. Use the exam bridge for auction payments, truthfulness, and worked social-choice rules.

game theory: given the rules, predict behaviour. mechanism design: given desired behaviour, build the rules.

θᵢ is private. everything else is common knowledge. that asymmetry is the entire subject.

11.1 The general setting

In one line

Mechanism design is game theory run backwards: instead of solving a given game, you design the game so that rational, self-interested players produce the outcome you wanted.

ObjectMeaningWho knows it
N = {1,…,n}agents, rational and intelligentcommon knowledge
Xset of alternatives / outcomescommon knowledge
θᵢ ∈ Θᵢagent i's type — the private signal fixing their preferencesagent i only
Θ = Θ₁ × ⋯ × Θₙset of type profiles; a typical one is θ = (θ₁,…,θₙ)the sets are common knowledge
P ∈ Δ(Θ)common prior over typescommon knowledge
pᵢ : Θᵢ → Δ(Θ₋ᵢ)individual beliefs, derived from P — consistency of beliefsderived
uᵢ : X × Θᵢ → ℝpayoff from outcome x to an agent of type θᵢthe function is common knowledge

Everything is common knowledge except the realised value of each θᵢ. That single piece of hidden information is what creates the design problem: agents may misreport their type if it pays, so the rules have to make honesty profitable.

11.2 Social choice functions

Sheet, Definition 48 A SOCIAL CHOICE FUNCTION is a map f : Θ₁ × ⋯ × Θₙ → X assigning to each type profile (θ₁,…,θₙ) an outcome from X. The outcome f(θ) is the social choice / collective choice for that profile.

An SCF is the goal, not the mechanism: it says what should happen for each combination of private types, and the designer's job is to build rules under which self-interested play produces exactly that. Two concrete instances you already know:

SettingTypes θᵢOutcomes XSCF
Second-price auctionvaluations vᵢ(who wins, what everyone pays)allocate to the highest valuation; winner pays the second-highest
Votingpreference orderingscandidatesa voting rule — plurality, Borda, and so on
Why the second-price auction is the standard example

Truthful bidding is weakly dominant (§2.2), so the mechanism implements the efficient SCF "give the item to the agent with the highest valuation" without needing to know anyone's valuation. That is the whole ambition of mechanism design, achieved in a single line of rules.

check

Why is a common prior P ∈ Δ(Θ) assumed?

It makes beliefs consistent: each agent's belief pᵢ(θᵢ) about the others is the conditional of a single shared distribution. Without it agents could hold mutually contradictory beliefs and the analysis loses its footing.

Is a social choice function a strategy?

No. A strategy maps your own information to your own action. An SCF maps the whole profile of types to a social outcome — it is the designer's objective, not a player's plan.

Sheet: Mechanism Design setting, Definition 48.

Let p=P1(A), q=P2(A). P1 gets 1+q from either row. P2 gets 1+p from either column. Therefore EVERY (p,q) ∈ [0,1]² is a Nash equilibrium. Both mixed maxmin and minmax values are 1. Every own mixture is maxmin. To minmax P1, P2 uses q=0. To minmax P2, P1 uses p=0.

Takeaway: 0=0 means an indifference condition holds for every probability; 0=nonzero means impossible. A singular system can describe a whole family.

13.2Backward induction and complete strategies

Tree methods · reference page 1; backward induction must be understood

  1. At each final decision node, select the action maximising the payoff of the player who moves there.
  2. Replace that continuation by its payoff and move backwards.
  3. State every prescribed action, including actions at unreached nodes.
  4. For ties, retain each best action; there may be multiple solutions.

An information set joins nodes a player cannot distinguish. You cannot choose different actions at nodes in the same information set. A proper subgame cannot cut through an information set.

Practice. P1 chooses L/R. P2 observes. After L, a gives (3,1), b gives (0,0). After R, a gives (2,2), b gives (1,4).

Solution: tree → strategies → SPE
P2 chooses a after L (1>0), b after R (4>2). P1 compares L→(3,1) with R→(1,4), so chooses L. SPE: (L, ab), where ab means “a after L, b after R”. Outcome (L,a), payoffs (3,1). P2 has four pure strategies: aa, ab, ba, bb. Normal-form PSNE: (L,aa), (L,ab), (R,bb). Only (L,ab) is subgame perfect.

2025 Q1C / 2023 tree. P2 chooses a₁,…,a₄; P1’s four nodes belong to one information set with L/R. P1 has only two pure strategies, not 16. Terminal histories are (aⱼ,L),(aⱼ,R), j=1,…,4. Proper subhistories: ε and (aⱼ). The strategic matrix has two P1 rows and four P2 columns; every L cell pays (1,−1), every R cell (−1,1).

13.3Zero-sum games: primal, dual, and a repeated PYQ

Not fully supplied by the four-page formula sheet

A is the row player’s payoff matrix; row maximises and column minimises. These LPs apply to this zero-sum formulation, not directly to arbitrary bimatrix games.

ROW (primal): maximise v subject to Σᵢ pᵢ Aᵢⱼ ≥ v for EVERY column j; Σᵢ pᵢ = 1; pᵢ ≥ 0. v is unrestricted in sign. COLUMN (dual): minimise w subject to Σⱼ Aᵢⱼ qⱼ ≤ w for EVERY row i; Σⱼ qⱼ = 1; qⱼ ≥ 0. w is unrestricted in sign. At the optimum, v=w.

13.4Core, Shapley, voting: short exam solutions

2025 Q3C, Q4B–C, Q5A · reference pages 3–4

Core = efficiency plus every coalition’s lower bound. If coalition values are costs instead of benefits, specify a cost-allocation model; the stability inequalities reverse. Do not silently use revenue inequalities for a cost game.

Benefit game: Σᵢ xᵢ=v(N); Σᵢ∈C xᵢ≥v(C). Three players: Lᵢ=v({i}), Uᵢ=v(N)−v(N\{i}). Core nonempty iff every Lᵢ≤Uᵢ and ΣLᵢ≤v(N)≤ΣUᵢ.

2025 Q5A: four players; every pair has value 30, grand coalition 50, singleton/triple values 0. Show emptiness without drawing.

Two constraints prove an empty core
x₁+x₂≥30 and x₃+x₄≥30 imply Σxᵢ≥60. Efficiency requires Σxᵢ=50. Contradiction: core is empty.

2025 Q4B: v(12)=v(13)=v(123)=300; all other coalitions have value 0. Compute the Shapley value.

Properties: superadditivity tests disjoint coalitions; convexity tests all pairs (or increasing marginal contributions). One violated inequality disproves a property; one satisfied inequality does not prove it. For three players, check all three singleton-pair unions and all three pair-pair overlaps, plus singleton pairs.

Voting: Shapley–Shubik = pivotal permutations / n!. Banzhaf absolute = swing count / 2ⁿ⁻¹; normalised Banzhaf = swing count / total swings. State which version you use. A 0/1 game must be checked for monotonicity before interpreting its Shapley value as conventional voting power.

13.5Bayesian equilibrium: types change the strategy set

2025 Q3A and May 2022 Q2A · procedure beyond the sheet

A type is private information about a player’s preferences/payoffs. A pure Bayesian strategy specifies an action for every possible type. With types I/U and actions A/B, player 2 has four pure plans: AA, AB, BA, BB (first letter for I).

P1 chooses a best response to expected payoff: E[u₁(a,s₂(t))] = Σₜ P(t) u₁(a,s₂(t);t). Each type t of P2 must best respond using its OWN payoff matrix. With correlated types, use conditional beliefs P(t₋ᵢ|tᵢ).

Worked training example (explicit assumptions). P(I)=3/4. P1’s payoffs are [[2,0],[0,1]] in both states. P2’s payoff matrix is [[1,0],[0,2]] for I and [[0,2],[1,0]] for U. Rows/columns are A,B.

Find both pure Bayesian Nash equilibria
If P1 plays A: type I chooses A (1>0), type U chooses B (2>0). Against plan AB, P1 gets 2·3/4=3/2 from A, 1·1/4=1/4 from B. Pure BNE: (A, AB). If P1 plays B: type I chooses B (2>0), type U chooses A (1>0). Against plan BA, P1 gets 2·1/4=1/2 from A, 1·3/4=3/4 from B. Pure BNE: (B, BA). These exhaust the PURE equilibria; mixed Bayesian equilibria require a separate support analysis.
Past-paper ambiguity

2025 Q3A names interested/uninterested types but prints only one payoff matrix. The training example above supplies an explicit U matrix; it is not claimed as the unique answer to that incomplete question. If data are missing in the exam, clearly state a defensible assumption as the paper permits.

Let p=P1(A), q=P2(A). Let a,b,c,d be joint probabilities of AA,AB,BA,BB. Always write a,b,c,d≥0 and a+b+c+d=1.

1. All independent mixed-strategy payoffs: (4pq+3(1−p)q+(1−p)(1−q), pq+3(1−p)q+4(1−p)(1−q)), 0≤p,q≤1. 2. Nash payoff set: {(4,1),(1,4),(2,2)}. Pure NE: AA, BB. Interior NE: p=q=1/2. 3. All correlated payoffs: (4a+3c+d, a+3c+4d), a,b,c,d≥0, sum=1. Equivalently conv{(4,1),(0,0),(3,3),(1,4)}. 4. Individually rational correlated payoffs: The same correlated set restricted to u₁≥1 and u₂≥1. P1 guarantees 1 by B; P2 guarantees 1 by A. 5. Correlated-equilibrium payoffs: The same payoff map with a≥b, d≥c, a≥c, d≥b. These are the four obey-versus-deviate constraints.

Derive one: P1 recommended A: a(4−3)+b(0−1)≥0, hence a≥b. Derive the other three similarly. Do not confuse a convex hull of all outcomes with the set of equilibrium outcomes.

Quick check: is probability 1 on BA a CE?

No. It yields (3,3) and is individually rational, but P1 can switch from B to A and get 4. The constraint d≥c becomes 0≥1, false.

13.8GVA/VCG payments and mechanism-design answers

2025 Q5B–C; July 2022 Q5A procurement

Forward combinatorial auction: allocate disjoint bundles to maximise total reported value. A bidder’s VCG payment is the harm their presence causes the other bidders.

pᵢ = (maximum welfare attainable by others WITHOUT i) − (welfare received by others in the chosen allocation WITH i). Utility = own value of allocated bundle − payment. Unallocated bidders pay 0 under the usual Clarke pivot rule.

2025 Q5B:

Bidder{1}{2}{1,2}
161010
