3809
Allocation, tie-breaking, payments, utilities
Best welfare = 18: item 2→bidder 1 and item 1→bidder 2 or 3. Choose bidder 2 by a fixed tie-breaking rule. Without bidder 1: best = 8 (bidder 3, item 1) + 5 (bidder 2, item 2) = 13. p₁ = 13 − 8 = 5. Without bidder 2: best = 10 (bidder 1, item 2) + 8 (bidder 3, item 1) = 18. p₂ = 18 − 10 = 8. p₃=0. Utilities: bidder 1 = 10−5=5; bidder 2 = 8−8=0; bidder 3=0.

Reverse auction / procurement: choose a feasible cover of the requested items with minimum total cost. With XOR bids, at most one bid from each seller may be selected. A winning seller receives:

payment to seller i = minimum cost WITHOUT i − cost of the OTHER winners WITH i. Seller utility = payment received − true cost. Assume a feasible alternative exists without i; otherwise flag the missing outside option.
TermMeaning you must demonstrate
DSICTruth is optimal for every report of others (weak dominance).
BICTruth maximises expected utility given one’s type and beliefs, when others report truthfully.
Ex-post efficient (EPE)Chosen outcome is Pareto efficient for each realised type profile; with quasilinear transfers, efficient allocation maximises total value.
Individually rational (IR)Participation utility is at least the outside option, commonly 0.
DictatorialA fixed player’s top choice is always selected (with fixed tie-breaking).

2025 Q5C SCF examples. P1 values x,y,z as (100,50,20) for a₁ and (50,100,40) for b₁. P2 values them as (0,50,100) for a₂ and (50,30,100) for b₂.

Two explicit rules and their checks

EPE + DSIC + dictatorial: choose x if P1 reports a₁, y if P1 reports b₁, ignoring P2. P1 receives their unique best outcome for each true type, so cannot gain by lying; P2 cannot affect the outcome. The unique top outcome of P1 cannot be Pareto dominated.

Not EPE + DSIC + non-dictatorial: always choose y. Reports have no effect, so truth is weakly optimal. It is not a dictatorship: y is not P1’s top at a₁ and never P2’s top. At (a₁,b₂), x=(100,50) strictly Pareto dominates y=(50,30), so the rule is not EPE.

Single-item formats: first price: winner pays own bid; second price: winner pays highest rival bid; English: ascending; Dutch: descending. Standard private-value second-price truthfulness follows by comparing your value v with the highest rival bid m: win if v>m, lose if v<m, indifferent at equality. State private-value/quasilinear assumptions.

13.9Bargaining and the final short-answer pass

Use reference page 3; older papers add bargaining and short concepts

Nash bargaining: maximise (x₁−d₁)(x₂−d₂) over feasible x with x≥d. On a polygon, check each efficient edge and relevant endpoints; do not assume the maximiser is a vertex.

Example: x₁+x₂≤60, d=(10,20). Surplus = 60−10−20=30. Split gains equally: x=(25,35). Nash product=15×15=225; total=60. On x₁+2x₂≤40, d=(4,2): NBS=(20,10), product=128.

Simple egalitarian solution: with the equal-payoff convention, choose the largest feasible t with x₁=x₂=t (and check individual rationality). An equal-gains convention instead uses x₁−d₁=x₂−d₂. State which convention the course/question uses; they differ when d₁≠d₂. On x₁+x₂≤60 with d=(10,20), equal payoffs gives (30,30), equal gains gives (25,35).

ConceptExam-ready distinction
Perfect vs imperfect informationPerfect: each information set is a singleton. Imperfect: a player cannot distinguish some decision nodes.
Complete vs incomplete informationComplete: payoff structure/types are known. Incomplete: some payoff-relevant type is private.
Mutual vs common knowledgeEveryone knows E vs everyone knows E, knows that everyone knows E, and so on indefinitely.
Braess paradoxAdding a link can worsen equilibrium travel time because route choices change; compare equilibria before and after the link.
Tragedy of the commonsA private gain is enjoyed individually while resource damage is shared, potentially creating excessive use.
Ordinal vs cardinal utilityRanking suffices for pure best replies. Expected utilities require meaningful payoff differences; positive affine transformations preserve mixed equilibria.
NucleolusLexicographically minimises sorted coalition excesses e(C,x)=v(C)−Σᵢ∈C xᵢ over the imputation set; if the core is nonempty it lies in the core.
Repeated / stochastic gamesRepeated: the stage game recurs; future rewards and punishments can matter. Stochastic: actions also affect state transitions. Distinguish the concepts; no time for lengthy proofs here.

Leave for extra time: long proofs, general balancedness derivations, exhaustive large-support calculations and extended application stories. Keep the original chapters for lookup.

1 · Pure/mixed equilibrium · 2 marks

12.1 Non-cooperative

Q1 — extensive form → strategic form

Q. Player 1 moves first, choosing L or R. Player 2 observes and then chooses a or b. Payoffs: (L,a) = (3,1), (L,b) = (0,0), (R,a) = (2,2), (R,b) = (1,4). Give the strategic form and all PSNE.

Strategy counts

Player 1 has one information set with two actions: |S₁| = 2. Player 2 has two information sets (after L, after R), two actions each: |S₂| = 4, written xy = (reply to L, reply to R).

The matrix

S₂ = {aa, ab, ba, bb}.
Row L: (3,1) (3,1) (0,0) (0,0)
Row R: (2,2) (1,4) (2,2) (1,4)

PSNE

Underline. Column aa: 3 > 2 → L. Row L against aa: player 2 gets 1; switching to ba gives 0 — so aa and ab both best. Working through: (L, aa), (L, ab) and (R, bb) are pure Nash equilibria. Only (L, ab) survives backward induction, since after R player 2 strictly prefers b (4 > 2) and after L prefers a (1 > 0).

Q2 — dominance grading

Q. For (3,3) (1,4) / (3,1) (0,0), state whether player 1's row A dominates row B, and at which grade.

Working

Column 1: u₁(A,·) = 3, u₁(B,·) = 3 — equal, not strict. Column 2: 1 > 0 — strict. Weak everywhere plus one strict ⇒ A weakly dominates B. Not strongly, because of the tie in column 1.

Q3 — full solution of a 2 × 2

Q. For (4,1) (0,4) / (1,5) (1,1): find all PSNE, both maxmin and minmax values for both players, and the MSNE.

PSNE

Column A: player 1 prefers A (4 > 1). Row A: player 2 prefers B (4 > 1). Column B: player 1 prefers B (1 > 0). Row B: player 2 prefers A (5 > 1). Best replies cycle — no PSNE.

Security values

Player 1: row minima min(4,0)=0, min(1,1)=1 → v̲₁ = 1, strategy B. Column maxima max(4,1)=4, max(0,1)=1 → v̄₁ = 1, forced by player 2 playing B.
Player 2 (on u₂): column minima min(1,5)=1, min(4,1)=1 → v̲₂ = 1. Row maxima max(1,4)=4, max(5,1)=5 → v̄₂ = 4, forced by player 1 playing A.

MSNE

Let player 1 play A with probability p. Player 2 indifferent: 1p + 5(1−p) = 4p + 1(1−p) → 5 − 4p = 1 + 3p → 7p = 4, p = 4/7. Let player 2 play A with probability q. Player 1 indifferent: 4q + 0(1−q) = 1q + 1(1−q) → 4q = 1, q = 1/4. So σ₁ = (4/7, 3/7), σ₂ = (1/4, 3/4). Player 1's payoff 4(1/4) = 1; player 2's 1(4/7) + 5(3/7) = 19/7.

Q4 — graphical method

Q. Zero-sum, payoffs to Rose: [2, −3 ; 0, 2 ; −5, 10] (three rows, two columns). Find optimal strategies and the value.

Working

No saddle point (maxmin = max(−3, 0, −5) = 0; minmax = min(2, 10) = 2; they differ). Draw the three lines against Colin's mixture x on B; the lowest point of the upper envelope is where the rows A and B lines cross. Solve [2, −3 ; 0, 2] by oddments: Rose (2/7, 5/7) on {A, B}, Colin (5/7, 2/7), value 4/7.

Verification

Rose C against Colin's optimum: (5/7)(−5) + (2/7)(10) = −5/7 < 4/7, so C is correctly excluded. Answer: Rose (2/7, 5/7, 0), Colin (5/7, 2/7), v = 4/7.

Q5 — correlated equilibrium

Q. For chicken (0,0) (7,2) / (2,7) (6,6), verify that α putting 1/3 on each of (D,C), (C,D) and (C,C) is a correlated equilibrium, and compare with the mixed Nash payoff.

Constraints

P1 told D (only cell (D,C) has weight): ⅓[u₁(D,C) − u₁(C,C)] = ⅓[7 − 6] = ⅓ ≥ 0 ✓.
P1 told C (cells (C,D), (C,C)): ⅓[u₁(C,D) − u₁(D,D)] + ⅓[u₁(C,C) − u₁(D,C)] = ⅓[2−0] + ⅓[6−7] = ⅓ ≥ 0 ✓.
Both player-2 constraints are symmetric and give ⅓ ≥ 0 ✓. All four hold.

Payoffs

⅓(7,2) + ⅓(2,7) + ⅓(6,6) = (5, 5). The MSNE has p(D) = q(D) = 1/3 and payoffs (14/3, 14/3) ≈ (4.67, 4.67). The correlated equilibrium is strictly better for both, and lies outside the convex hull of the pure equilibrium payoffs.

12.2 Cooperative

Q6 — imputations

Q. v(1)=10, v(2)=20, v(3)=30, v(123)=100. Is (15, 25, 60) an imputation? Is (5, 35, 60)?

Working

(15, 25, 60): sums to 100 ✓, and 15 ≥ 10, 25 ≥ 20, 60 ≥ 30 ✓ — an imputation.
(5, 35, 60): sums to 100 ✓ but x₁ = 5 < v({1}) = 10 ✗ — individual rationality fails, so not an imputation.

Q7 — the core

Q. v(1)=v(2)=v(3)=0, v(12)=100, v(13)=60, v(23)=40, v(123)=120. Find the core.

Ceilings

x₃ ≤ 120 − 100 = 20; x₂ ≤ 120 − 60 = 60; x₁ ≤ 120 − 40 = 80. Sum = 160 > 120, so the core has positive area — a polygon, not a point.

Description

The core is { (x₁,x₂,x₃) : x₁+x₂+x₃ = 120, 0 ≤ x₁ ≤ 80, 0 ≤ x₂ ≤ 60, 0 ≤ x₃ ≤ 20 }. Its vertices are found by binding pairs of constraints, for example (80, 20, 20), (80, 40, 0), (60, 60, 0), (40, 60, 20).

Q8 — Shapley value

Q. Same game as Q7. Compute the Shapley value and say whether it lies in the core.

By orderings

Marginal contributions:
123: (0, 100, 20) · 132: (0, 60, 60) · 213: (100, 0, 20)
231: (80, 0, 40) · 312: (60, 60, 0) · 321: (80, 40, 0)
Column sums: 320, 260, 140. Divide by 6: φ = (160/3, 130/3, 70/3) ≈ (53.3, 43.3, 23.3). Check: they sum to 360/3 = 120 ✓.

In the core?

Test the binding constraint x₁ + x₂ ≥ 100: 160/3 + 130/3 = 290/3 ≈ 96.7 < 100 ✗. Coalition {1,2} blocks, so the Shapley value is not in the core here — consistent with the game being superadditive but not convex.

Q9 — power indices

Q. For [51; 50, 49, 1] compute the Shapley–Shubik and normalised Banzhaf indices.

Winning coalitions

{1,2} = 99 ✓, {1,3} = 51 ✓, {1,2,3} ✓. {2,3} = 50 ✗. Player 1 is in every winning coalition — a veto player.

Shapley–Shubik

Player 1 is pivotal in 4 of the 6 orderings (every ordering where 1 is not first, plus none where 1 is first since {1} already loses — check each: 123→2 pivotal, 132→3 pivotal, 213→1, 231→1, 312→1, 321→1). So φ = (4/6, 1/6, 1/6) = (2/3, 1/6, 1/6).

Banzhaf

Player 1's swings: C = {2} ✓, {3} ✓, {2,3} ✓, ∅ ✗ → ψ₁ = 3/4. Player 2's: only C = {1} ✓ → 1/4. Same for player 3. Raw (3/4, 1/4, 1/4), total 5/4, normalised (3/5, 1/5, 1/5). The two indices disagree — worth stating explicitly.

Q10 — bargaining

Q. F = {(x₁,x₂) : x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 40, x ≥ 0}, v = (4, 2). Find the Nash bargaining solution.

Working

Frontier x₁ = 40 − 2x₂. Maximise g(x₂) = (40 − 2x₂ − 4)(x₂ − 2) = (36 − 2x₂)(x₂ − 2).
g′ = −2(x₂ − 2) + (36 − 2x₂) = 40 − 4x₂ = 0 → x₂ = 10, x₁ = 20.
Check feasibility 20 + 20 = 40 ✓ and x ≥ v ✓. Nash product = 16 × 8 = 128.

Q11 — game structure identification

Q. Classify v(1)=1, v(2)=1, v(3)=1, v(12)=3, v(13)=3, v(23)=3, v(123)=6 as monotonic / superadditive / essential / convex.

Working

Monotonic ✓ — 1 ≤ 3 ≤ 6 along every chain.
Superadditive ✓ — v(12) = 3 ≥ 1 + 1; v(123) = 6 ≥ v(12) + v(3) = 4.
Essential ✓ — Σ v({i}) = 3 ≠ 6.
Convex: take C = {1,2}, D = {1,3}. v(123) + v(1) = 6 + 1 = 7 ≥ v(12) + v(13) = 6 ✓. Other pairs give the same or slack, so ✓ convex — hence the core is non-empty and contains the Shapley value (2, 2, 2).

Q12 — short answers

Every dominant strategy equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium. True or false?

True. Best response against every profile implies best response against the equilibrium profile.

A finite game always has a pure strategy Nash equilibrium.

False. Matching pennies has none. Every finite game has a mixed one (Nash's theorem).

The minmax value of a player is at most their maxmin value.

False — the inequality runs the other way, v̲ᵢ ≤ v̄ᵢ.

The order of eliminating strictly dominated strategies affects the outcome.

False for strict dominance. True for weak and very weak.

The core of a convex game may be empty.

False. Proposition 5 exhibits a core element for any convex game.

Every correlated equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium.

False — the containment is the other way: every NE induces a CE, but chicken has a CE with payoffs no NE achieves.

In a second-price auction, bidding your valuation is strongly dominant.

False — weakly dominant. When you lose either way the payoffs tie at zero.

Mixed strategy equilibria need only ordinal utilities.

False. Mixing probabilities are ratios of payoff differences, so cardinal (interval-scale) utilities are required. Ordinal utilities also suffice for pure best responses and pure Nash equilibrium; expected-utility mixtures require cardinal utility information.

The bar convention, one last time

The underbar goes with maxmin — the lower guarantee you secure for yourself. The overbar goes with minmax — the upper ceiling others can impose. v̲ᵢ ≤ v̄ᵢ. If you remember only one thing about Part 04, remember which bar is which.
